title: Sheinbaum Visits the People’s Hospital in China’s Nanshan District
author: Angeles Cruz Martínez
content:
_This article by[Angeles Cruz
Martínez](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Angeles%20Cruz%20Mart%C3%ADnez%2C%20enviada),
special correspondent, originally appeared in the [November 18, 2026 edition
of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/11/18/politica/sheinbaum-
visita-el-hospital-popular-del-distrito-de-nanshan-en-china), Mexico's premier
left wing daily newspaper._

**Shenzhen.** To learn about China’s health system and bring best practices
suited to Mexico’s circumstances back to the country, President Claudia
Sheinbaum visited the People’s Hospital in Nanshan District.

Upon leaving, she said the hospital was “very impressive for its capacity to
provide care, the amount of equipment and the use of artificial intelligence
to make clinical diagnoses and even determine treatments.”

During the nearly two-hour tour, the president was able to observe how blood
tests, sample collection and the delivery of medicines by robots are carried
out.

She said there is an intention to **bring these technological advances to
Mexico**. To that end, her administration will work with the Chinese embassy
in Mexico.

She stressed that China’s health system is similar to Mexico’s, as it has all
three levels of care, but here, she emphasized, “the capacity to provide care
is extraordinary.”

Nanshan People’s Hospital is a highly specialized facility, and although it is
80 years old, it has been modernized over time and in 2024 earned level five
smart hospital accreditation. According to information from the hospital, it
has electronic medical records and medical services with a digital system.

It also has a big data research center and promoted the establishment of the
Smart Healthcare Innovation Center in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Bay Area.

Separately, Health Secretary David Kershenobich said that, beyond what they
were able to learn at Nanshan Hospital, Mexico’s government is interested in
China’s health system because of the effective functioning of its primary care
and its traditional medicine.

Here, people seek services to prevent disease, and “that is what we want, in
addition to finding a way to institutionalize traditional medicine,” as the
Asian giant has done, he said.

The official is accompanying President Sheinbaum on her visit to China, which
has included visits to hospitals.

Kershenobich visited a center that offers traditional Chinese and allopathic
medicine.

In an interview, the official said that in China, primary care is guaranteed
through visits to people’s homes. This has already begun, in some form, in
Mexico, with house-to-house visits to older adults, but for the management of
medical conditions.

A culture of prevention still needs to be instilled so that people visit
health facilities at least once a year to check their blood pressure, blood
sugar levels and weight, among other indicators.

He said that in China, people pay a nominal annual fee for a basic package of
services, which acts as an incentive for them to look after their health,
because in most cases they go to prevent disease, not to treat it.

In Mexico, medical services are free, but “we lack a culture of prevention,
social contagion.”

With that objective, **12,000 first-contact medical offices will begin
operating in 2027** , he said.

Regarding traditional medicine, Kershenobich highlighted the Chinese system
and, above all, its coexistence with allopathic medicine. Doctors also receive
university training that includes millennia-old traditional knowledge in
different areas, including midwifery. This, too, is something of interest to
bring to Mexico.

China also has a very strong traditional medicine industry, which we do not
have, but “it can be developed based on our cultural and Indigenous wealth.”

Kershenobich mentioned the case of the municipality of Jesús María, Nayarit,
where there is a hospital in which half the services involve traditional
medicine and the other half allopathic medicine.

He emphasized that the Universal Health Service is designed to promote disease
prevention so that fewer people need hospital care, incorporating the
knowledge of Indigenous peoples.

The difference is that in China the system is “very well organized and
established.” He said efforts would be made to bring that model to Mexico to
institutionalize traditional medicine and, at the same time, **advance
digitalization through electronic medical records** , which are fundamental to
developing medicine in the future in Mexico and worldwide.
